Predict Missing or Future Links in a Network

Source: R/link_prediction.R
predict_links.Rd

predict_links() scores every pair of nodes for how strongly the network's structure suggests a link between them, with one or more similarity indices: common neighbours, resource allocation, Adamic-Adar, Jaccard, preferential attachment and Katz (Liben-Nowell & Kleinberg, 2007). It returns one row per pair and index, ranked within each index, and a consensus ranking across the indices. It takes a netobject, a cograph_network, a tna model or a square weight matrix, weighted or binary, directed or undirected.

A high score says that a pair resembles linked pairs in the network's structure (shared neighbours, busy endpoints, many connecting paths), not that the link exists in the population or will form. The indices are heuristics and often disagree; the consensus rank shows the pairs on which they agree. How well an index recovers links is measured by scoring held-out edges with evaluate_links(); pathways() writes the top predictions as pathway strings.

Usage

predict_links(
  x,
  methods = c("common_neighbors", "resource_allocation", "adamic_adar", "jaccard",
    "preferential_attachment", "katz"),
  weighted = TRUE,
  top_n = NULL,
  exclude_existing = TRUE,
  include_self = FALSE,
  katz_damping = NULL
)

# S3 method for class 'net_link_prediction'
print(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'net_link_prediction'
summary(object, ...)

Arguments

x

The network: a netobject, a cograph_network, a tna model, or a numeric square weight matrix. A network keeps its own direction; a matrix or tna model is directed unless it is symmetric. A netobject_group or an mcml raises an error of class nestimate_bad_input: predict each network separately. For the print() method: a predict_links() result.

methods

The indices to compute, one or more of "common_neighbors", "resource_allocation", "adamic_adar", "jaccard", "preferential_attachment" and "katz" (defined under Details). By default all six.

weighted

Whether common neighbours, resource allocation, Adamic-Adar and Jaccard use the edge weights (TRUE, default) or the binary adjacency (FALSE). Preferential attachment, Katz and the degrees that resource allocation and Adamic-Adar divide by always use the binary adjacency.

top_n

The number of predictions kept per index, the highest scores. Default NULL (every pair). The ranks are computed before the cut, so they stay the same.

exclude_existing

Whether pairs that already have an edge are left out of the predictions. Default TRUE.

include_self

Whether self-pairs (a node with itself) are listed for a directed network; an undirected network never lists them. All indices score self-pairs 0. It also decides whether self-loops count in the number of existing edges. Default FALSE.

katz_damping

The attenuation factor \(\beta\) of the Katz index. Default NULL, which uses \(0.9 / \rho(A)\) for the spectral radius \(\rho(A)\) of the adjacency (0.1 when it is 0). A value at or above \(1 / \rho(A)\), where the series diverges, is replaced by \(0.9 / \rho(A)\) with a warning.

...

For the print() and summary() methods: not used.

object

For summary(): a predict_links() result.

Value

A net_link_prediction object. print() lists the top ten predicted links (by consensus rank with several indices, by score with one) and returns its input invisibly. summary() returns a data frame with one row per index: method, n_predictions, and the score_mean, score_sd, score_max and score_min of its predictions; an index with no predictions (every possible link already exists) has n_predictions = 0 and NA scores. evaluate_links() scores the predictions against known edges, and pathways() writes them as pathway strings. The object's fields:

predictions

Data frame, one row per node pair and index: from, to, method, score, existing (whether the pair already has an edge) and rank, sorted by score (highest first) within each index. An undirected network lists each pair once.

consensus

Data frame, one row per node pair: from, to, avg_rank (the pair's mean rank over the indices that list it), n_methods (how many do) and consensus_rank, ordered by avg_rank. NULL when only one index was computed.

scores

Named list of score matrices, one per index.

adjacency

The 0/1 adjacency matrix of the input network.

methods

The indices computed.

nodes

The node names.

directed, weighted

Whether the network was read as directed, and whether weights were used.

n_nodes

The number of nodes.

n_existing

The number of existing edges: non-zero cells of the adjacency matrix, each undirected edge counted once, self-loops counted only with include_self = TRUE.

Details

Methods

common_neighbors

The number of shared neighbours. For a directed network, shared out-neighbours plus shared in-neighbours, computed as A %*% t(A) + t(A) %*% A.

resource_allocation

Zhou et al. (2009). Like common neighbours, but each shared neighbour z is weighted by 1/degree(z) (in- plus out-degree for a directed network). It penalises hubs and rewards rare shared connections.

adamic_adar

Adamic & Adar (2003). Like resource allocation, but weighted by 1/log(degree(z)), a milder penalty; a neighbour of degree 1 adds nothing.

jaccard

Shared neighbours divided by all neighbours of the two nodes. With weighted = TRUE it is the weighted Jaccard (Ruzicka) index, \(\sum_z \min(|w_{iz}|, |w_{jz}|) / \sum_z \max(|w_{iz}|, |w_{jz}|)\), which equals the binary index on 0/1 weights and lies between 0 and 1. For a directed network, computed on the combined (out + in) neighbourhoods, each neighbour weighted by the larger of its two directions.

preferential_attachment

The source's out-degree times the target's in-degree (Barabasi & Albert, 1999): the "rich get richer" effect.

katz

Katz (1953). A sum over all paths between the two nodes, damped exponentially by path length, computed by matrix inversion as (I - beta * A)^{-1} - I. It reads the global structure. If the inversion fails, the series is truncated after six terms.

Every index is computed with matrix operations on the whole network at once.

References

Liben-Nowell, D. & Kleinberg, J. (2007). The link-prediction problem for social networks. JASIST, 58(7), 1019–1031.

Zhou, T., Lu, L. & Zhang, Y.-C. (2009). Network topology and link prediction. European Physical Journal B, 71, 623–630.

Adamic, L. A. & Adar, E. (2003). Friends and neighbors on the Web. Social Networks, 25(3), 211–230.

Katz, L. (1953). A new status index derived from sociometric analysis. Psychometrika, 18(1), 39–43.

Jaccard, P. (1901). Etude comparative de la distribution florale dans une portion des Alpes et des Jura. Bulletin de la Societe Vaudoise des Sciences Naturelles, 37, 547–579.

Ioffe, S. (2010). Improved consistent sampling, weighted minhash and L1 sketching. IEEE International Conference on Data Mining, 246–255.

Barabasi, A.-L. & Albert, R. (1999). Emergence of scaling in random networks. Science, 286(5439), 509–512.

See also

evaluate_links for prediction evaluation, build_network for network estimation.

Examples

seqs <- data.frame(
  V1 = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "A", "C", "E", "B"),
  V2 = c("B", "C", "D", "E", "C", "E", "A", "D"),
  V3 = c("C", "D", "E", "A", "D", "A", "B", "E")
)
net <- build_network(seqs, method = "relative")
pred <- predict_links(net)
print(pred)
#> Link Prediction  [directed | weighted | 5 nodes | 8 existing edges]
#>   Methods: common_neighbors, resource_allocation, adamic_adar, jaccard, preferential_attachment, katz
#> 
#>   Top predicted links (consensus across 6 methods):
#>     1. C -> B  (avg rank: 4.3, agreed: 6/6)
#>     2. B -> A  (avg rank: 4.8, agreed: 6/6)
#>     3. C -> A  (avg rank: 5.0, agreed: 6/6)
#>     4. D -> C  (avg rank: 5.5, agreed: 6/6)
#>     5. A -> D  (avg rank: 5.8, agreed: 6/6)
#>     6. D -> A  (avg rank: 6.2, agreed: 6/6)
#>     7. E -> D  (avg rank: 6.7, agreed: 6/6)
#>     8. E -> C  (avg rank: 7.5, agreed: 6/6)
#>     9. B -> E  (avg rank: 7.7, agreed: 6/6)
#>     10. A -> E  (avg rank: 7.8, agreed: 6/6)
#>     ... and 2 more predictions
summary(pred)
